stories.title: Could Alberta's vote on independence be Canada's Brexit moment?
stories.summary: WATCH: The BBC's Nadine Yousif meets the separatists who want to quit the country - and the Canadians calling for unity in the face of threats from US President Trump.

People in the province of Alberta will vote on 19 October on whether they want to start the process of separating from the rest of Canada.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has called the upcoming referendum a "dangerous bluff", comparing it to the Brexit vote that saw the UK leave the European Union.

But supporters of Albertan independence believe that the oil-rich province has long been overlooked by decision-makers in Ottawa, the national capital, and that federal environmental policies have hindered its ability to develop its natural resources.

So, could Alberta really become its own country?

The BBC's Nadine Yousif takes us on a journey through Alberta to talk to both supporters and opponents of separation about their hopes for the country's future.

stories.title: As U.S. blocks DJI, Insta360 races to win American creators
stories.summary: Regulatory clarity and market timing are a boon for smaller Chinese smart-camera maker Insta360 and its independent Antigravity drone brand.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
China Outside China

Regulatory clarity and market timing are a boon for smaller Chinese smart-camera maker Insta360 and its independent Antigravity drone brand.

Chinese camera maker Insta360 is hoping to gain U.S. market share while market leader DJI remains hampered by national security restrictions.

Insta360 is benefiting from the clarity of 2024 regulatory rules while DJI’s new products are barred from FCC approval.

Insta360 launched Antigravity as an independent drone brand in 2025, which was incubated in collaboration with third parties.

On a Saturday morning in September, dozens of people lined up in New York City’s Times Square to check out pocket-sized cameras made by Chinese camera maker Insta360. YouTubers flew in to promote the products. As part of the marketing campaign, cyclists prepared to bike around the city in bright yellow shirts emblazoned with the Insta360 logo.

The Shenzhen-based company was opening its first flagship store in the U.S., a high-profile push to market its smart cameras to content creators, travelers, and sports enthusiasts. It was also a statement of confidence in a market where Chinese technology companies are facing growing scrutiny.

There are restrictions, but it’s better to have a clear no than maybe in business.” Chris Pereira, founder of consultancy iMpact

“The U.S. is a super high potential market for us,” Max Richter, Insta360’s co-founder, told Rest of World at the store opening. The U.S. accounts for 30% to 40% of the company’s revenue, he said. “You have an amazing outdoor sports community, you have a huge influencer economy, and I think Insta360 really gathers both of these audiences.”

Insta360’s optimism and U.S. expansion stand in sharp contrast to the experience of DJI, the dominant Chinese player it’s trying to challenge in the global drone and handheld camera market. DJI dominates the global civilian drone market, while Insta360 last year announced a separate company to make drones. In handheld smart cameras, DJI accounted for 73% of the global shipments, while Insta360 accounted for 20%. California-based GoPro, the pioneer of action cameras, has been largely pushed out of the market .

Washington has increasingly treated DJI as a national security risk. The U.S. Department of Defense has labeled DJI a Chinese military company, a decision the company has been fighting for years . The Federal Communications Commission has blocked DJI from selling new drones as well as cameras in the U.S. In the meantime, Insta360 is racing to win American consumers.

Both companies are based in Shenzhen, but they took different paths to becoming rivals. DJI was founded in 2006 and quickly became the global leader in consumer drones, with most of its sales coming from overseas. It expanded into handheld stabilized cameras in 2016.

Insta360 was founded in 2015 as a camera company. Its early success came from 360-degree cameras, which capture a panoramic view, before the company expanded into stabilized cameras and microphones. Its founder JK Liu had said the company aimed at the global market from “day one,” with a particular emphasis on America. Richter, a German native, first moved to China with a German company. He then worked for DJI before joining Insta360.

Arrival of Antigravity

Insta360 recently entered the drone business. The company announced the launch of an independent drone brand, Antigravity, in 2025, which it said was incubated in collaboration with third parties. The move could help insulate Insta360’s camera business from any future restrictions targeting Chinese drones, Chris Pereira, founder of consultancy iMpact, which helps Chinese companies sell abroad, told Rest of World.

The FCC has banned new foreign-made drones from entering the U.S. market, though companies can apply for waivers if they plan to move manufacturing to America. Antigravity obtained FCC’s approval for its drone, A1, just before the rule took effect.

Michael Shabun, the Los Angeles-based chief executive of Antigravity, told Rest of World at the store opening that the company was planning to move its manufacturing from Asia to the U.S. in the coming years.

Antigravity is positioning the A1 drone, with a 360-degree camera, firmly as a consumer-facing product. Shabun said the company stores all U.S. user data locally and has designed the drone so that it cannot carry more than 50 grams of additional weight, a restriction intended to prevent misuse of the drone for purposes beyond leisure. “They’re built for fun; they’re built for content creation; they’re built for exploration,” he said.

DJI drones have been widely used by commercial operators and law enforcement agencies, making their potential cybersecurity and data-security risks a particular concern in Washington.

“People in the U.S. are more excited about our product than any other region. And the drone market in the U.S. is very sophisticated and developed,” Shabun said, adding that the A1 would be put on the shelves of the Insta360 store.

Lure of the American consumer

Even as the U.S. government ramps up scrutiny of Chinese businesses, Chinese companies are eager to bring their products to America, especially at a time of slowing consumer spending and rising competition at home. Over the past two years, New York City has seen a number of Chinese brands open new shops, from clothing brand Urban Revivo to bubble tea chain Mixue. DJI opened a store on Fifth Avenue in 2024.

In China, DJI and Insta360 have fought a fierce price war over their handheld camera products. The rising costs of memory chips have weighed on their profitability. In the first half of 2026, Insta360’s net profit dropped by 94% compared with a year ago. The two companies have also sued each other over intellectual property infringements.

In the U.S. market, Insta360 might enjoy an advantage. Pereira said the first batch of Chinese companies to gain prominence in America, such as telecoms equipment maker Huawei, social media platform TikTok, and DJI, had attracted intense scrutiny.

One of the big deciding factors was availability. I can go into a store and buy [Insta360].” Lars Kappler, a real estate consultant in San Diego

He said the “second wave” of Chinese brands — like Xiaomi and Xiaohongshu — enjoyed more clarity. “There are restrictions, but it’s better to have a clear no than maybe in business,” Pereira said.

DJI can still sell its existing drones and cameras in the U.S., but its future in the market is unclear. The 2024 National Defense Authorization Act passed by Congress required the FCC to add communications and video surveillance equipment made by DJI and another Chinese drone maker, Autel Robotics, to its Covered List, effectively barring the agency from authorizing new products from the companies. The FCC has not approved new DJI products since November.

In an email to Rest of World , an FCC spokesperson said DJI’s products were banned in accordance with 2024 law, while Insta360’s products were not added to the Covered List.

Insta360 has been able to register new products with the FCC while DJI is blocked. Asked whether the company could avoid the pressures facing DJI, Insta360 co-founder Richter said he was confident it would be able to stay in America. “There is no sensitive technology,” he said. “We fully comply with all regulators. There’s nothing to hide.”

Some of DJI’s loyal American users are already switching sides. Lars Kappler, a real estate consultant in San Diego, has been using a DJI camera for a year. He told Rest of World he recently bought three Insta360 cameras and a microphone for his social media videos, because DJI’s latest products were not released in the U.S. “One of the big deciding factors was availability,” Kappler said. “I can go into a store and buy [Insta360].”

Michael Alvarado, an auto-body technician in Minnesota, also recently switched from DJI to Insta360’s latest handheld vlogging camera, Luna Ultra, to film his everyday life and family trips. He liked Insta360’s new features, such as the detachable screen, and was also worried about DJI’s long-term prospects in the U.S.

“As much as I’m pissed about the whole ban,” Alvarado told Rest of World , “I’m going to focus on who has the win right now, and unfortunately that’s Insta360.”

The AI boom is making the world’s cheapest smartphones disappear

AI data centers are driving demand for memory chips, pushing phone makers to raise prices and abandon some of their most affordable models.

Who gets to decide if AI is safe? Africa wants a say

African companies race to adopt American and Chinese AI, with little attention paid to safety.

Not just AI. China is building technologies that challenge U.S. dominance

From batteries and solar panels to drones and satellites, China is building tech capabilities that extend well beyond AI, writes Steve Feldstein in his new book, "Bytes and Bullets: Global Rivalries, Big Tech, and the New Shape of Modern Warfare."

stories.body:
Just as Brown and Blair did in 2005, Andy Burnham aims to champion debt relief to help developing countries

Developing nations face triple shock, UN warns

F rom Washington to Paris, London to Tokyo, policymakers in every large economy have been counting the costs of bond market turmoil in recent weeks. But the brunt of the pain is being borne by heavily indebted developing countries that have little hope of influencing the whims of global investors, but pay the price regardless.

Markets have responded to the war in the Middle East, and a spendthrift White House, by dumping government bonds – driving up borrowing costs just about everywhere.

Finance ministers and central bankers gathering in Bangkok this week for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank may be loth to point the finger at Donald Trump’s regime, but all are at least in part hostage to the US president’s war plans.

That has made what was already a perilous situation even worse – just as the world is battling an energy crisis, and as developing countries urgently need to invest in adapting to the climate emergency.

Even before the latest market gyrations, experts calculated that debt servicing costs absorbed 45% of government revenues in the global south , and 70% in low-income countries. That crowds out desperately needed spending on public services and investing for the future.

There have been growing demands for reform of the framework for international debt in recent years, including from African Union heads of state , and under the G20 chairs of Brazil and South Africa.

The G20 – the forum in which Gordon Brown coordinated a global fiscal stimulus package in the depths of the financial crisis in spring 2009 – is meant to be an important body for discussing international economic issues. With a much wider membership than the G7, it has coordinated previous efforts on debt, including establishing the IMF-administered Common Framework, to which struggling countries can apply, and suspending repayments for hard-hit borrowers during the Covid crisis.

However, this year’s chair has been Trump’s US, which has placed much more emphasis on other aspects of the G20’s remit, including promoting global economic growth – somewhat ironically, given the main obstacle to achieving it is the war on Iran.

Next year, the presidency falls to the UK, and Labour has made clear it will have different priorities. These will include seeking a global agreement on AI regulation, which seems a faint hope but is clearly worth pursuing.

The UK also intends to put unsustainable debt on the agenda. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, who will be in Bangkok, told Labour conference delegates last month: “Friends, I promise this. We will use our G20 presidency next year to meet our responsibilities and mobilise the world, building on the great achievements on debt and development of the last Labour government.”

He was referring to 2005, when Brown and Tony Blair rode the vociferous Make Poverty History movement to the Gleneagles G8 summit and beyond, securing significant debt relief for more than 30 countries .

As the development minister, Kirsty McNeill, herself a veteran of that campaign, said recently, the circumstances now are very different, for two reasons. First, she said, “we’re now dealing with private creditors – the debt isn’t held by us. So that is quite a big shift.” And second, she suggested it was harder now to delineate a group of countries clearly deserving of support.

“There isn’t this really clear demarcation between the very poor world and the very rich world that was true when I was starting out, and it was just a much starker and therefore more readily told story because the antagonists and the protagonists were just much clearer,” she told an event at the Labour conference.

Yet she and other ministers have made clear they are open to proposals – and ready to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind making progress on this formidable challenge.

after newsletter promotion

One ambitious plan drawn up by the thinktank Development Finance International (DFI) and shared with the government would involve 27 of the most heavily burdened countries being given a 10-year “holiday” during which their debt service costs would be slashed to below 10% of their revenues.

Implemented by cutting interest rates and extending loan terms rather than writing off debt altogether, the $13bn-a-year cost would fall primarily on private creditors – which might have to be coaxed, cajoled, perhaps even legislated into taking part, as in previous debt relief initiatives.

The “hope initiative” also envisages potential relief for another six small island developing states that do not meet the threshold on the basis of their debt burden but are regularly battered by natural disasters. These could be offered a five-year “holiday” from the moment of the next extreme weather event they face, at the cost of a further $700m a year.

An even more expansive version would embrace another five countries, including Pakistan and Angola.

Crucially, because the international financial institutions – including the IMF and the World Bank – tend to be preferred creditors, only chipping in when other help is exhausted, the costs to them would be relatively low.

Echoing Andy Burnham’s slogan – so far confined to the domestic sphere – Matthew Martin, DFI’s executive director and the author of the plan, says: “Let’s bring hope back to the poorest countries in the world, through an ambitious but financially and politically feasible initiative, which will free up $13bn for them to spend on their climate and development goals.”

It remains to be seen how bold the government is prepared to be in setting its G20 agenda, but the groundwork is being done.

Labour trashed its reputation as a champion for international development when Keir Starmer took the axe to aid spending to pay for defence. Perhaps 2027 could be the year Burnham starts to rebuild it.

stories.body:
‘Even if AI supercharged the economy, its impact on the government’s finances would be muted’

Back through political history to the age of Ronald Reagan , Republicans have repeatedly promised the US public that tax cuts would pay for themselves, firing up economic growth and filling the government’s coffers.

The promise never really panned out. From the Gipper’s day on, the Republicans’ tax cuts inevitably increased the budget deficit. Despite its failure, though, the promise is back, coated in a fine new layer of artificial intelligence pixie dust. It will fail again.

The treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, is relying on an AI-laced economy when he promises to deliver annual economic growth of 3% – a rate that, except for the rebound from the Covid pandemic, has been achieved only twice this century. Dreams of AI inflect Donald Trump’s fantasy that “we’re growing at a faster rate than we’ve ever grown before,” which will allow the government to “take care of the 40 trillion ” in federal debt “over a period of time”.

Financial markets, however, are not buying. Last week, the yield on the 10-year treasury bond surged to its highest in almost a quarter century, more than a full percentage point higher than when Trump launched his misbegotten war against Iran.

The war’s inflationary impact is the most immediate cause of rising bond yields. It already persuaded the Fed to raise short-term interest rates. But the treasury market is also being walloped by the US’s unbalanced finances. There is no realistic path for economic growth to generate the tax revenues needed to fix the US’s enormous and growing budget deficit. Investors are demanding more to cover the growing funding gap.

Borrowing is likely to become more expensive still. Foreign central banks, which once reliably bought treasuries to build up foreign reserves and manage their exchange rates, have cut back on their exposure to US government debt. The treasury now relies largely on private investors seeking to turn a profit. It finds itself competing for their money with the very AI superscalers on which it is pinning its future hopes, which are borrowing hand over fist to fund the buildout of datacenters to train their agents.

Indeed, the US’s finances find themselves in a bit of a negative spiral, as rising bond yields put additional pressure on the budget. Interest payments on the federal debt alone are consuming 3.3% of GDP, up from an average of 2.1% over the preceding 50 years.

And Trump’s fiscal management – his One Big Beautiful Bill Act is estimated to add $4.7tn to the federal debt through 2035 – is not making the budget math easier. The deficit already hit 6% of GDP – twice the size Bessent once promised. The Congressional Budget Office projected it will close in on 7% of GDP by 2033. And that was before Trump promised a $5,000 “dividend” to every US adult if the GOP kept control of Congress in the midterms. There is no realistic amount of growth that can fill the fiscal hole that Trump keeps digging.

The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFPB) sketched out a few scenarios . Assuming the temporary tax cuts in Trump’s 2025 law are made permanent by a future Congress – an assumption that fits the historical pattern – and that the government does not recover the revenue lost when the supreme court struck down its national security tariffs, achieving a budget deficit of 3% of GDP by 2036 would require annual growth of 4.4% over the next decade. Achieving a balanced budget by then would require the economy to expand 7.2% per year.

It is not impossible for AI to deliver this kind of growth. Some economists are willing to contemplate scenarios in which artificial intelligence boosts economic growth to 15% per year, by taking over much of the cognitive work usually performed by humans. But these scenarios do not appear likely.

According to the CFRB, stabilizing the federal debt would require average growth in total factor productivity – a measure of how efficiently economic inputs are converted into goods and services – to hit 2.5% per year over the next decade. The US has only hit that once since 1959. And that is despite massive productivity gains over the period from electrification, the completion of the federal highway system, the telecommunications revolution and the first wave of IT and automation.

Even if AI supercharged the economy, its impact on the government’s finances would be muted, for it would massively shift the fruits of growth from labor to capital, and the tax rate on capital today is only about half the tax rate on labor. Moreover, such a shift in the distribution of economic spoils would probably call for massive government spending to sustain the livelihoods of the many workers left behind.

What can we expect from the AI-pixie dust? At the moment people seem particularly worried about AI agents slipping their enclosures and killing us all. But even short of that, it is not a given that their impact will be inevitably positive for the economy, not to say the government’s finances necessarily provide the money for the federal government to right its finances.

For one, their massive debt-fuelled investments are pushing interest rates higher, complicating government financing. Their future promise, moreover, also comes with momentous risk.

The Stanford economist Hanno Lustig estimates that for the owners of datacenters to break even on their massive investments in AI – estimated to reach $1.43tn this year – their revenue would have to grow by 45% on average every year for the next seven years. By 2032, it would amount to roughly 9.2% of GDP.

A similar analysis by Jared Bernstein, former chair of Joe Biden’s Council of Economic Advisers, and Stanford economist Ryan Cummings, concluded that the nation’s six superscalers – Google, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, SpaceX and Amazon – would need additional revenues of $13.1tn to $18.7tn over the next 10 years just to pay for their massive investments in AI. That is roughly the same as their total revenues over the last 10 years.

It’s hard to forecast precisely what would happen to financial markets were these targets to be missed. But it’s safe to say that it might complicate the task of trimming the budget deficit and financing the US’s vast public debt.

UK 'does not support' Trump-Putin diesel deal, says defence secretary Streeting

Published 3 hours ago

The UK does not support Donald Trump's deal with Vladimir Putin, which would see the US purchase millions of tonnes of diesel from Russia, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House, he said the agreement had been done in the context of the US president facing elections in November and at a time when politicians across the world were under pressure to ease the cost of living.

He argued that the US and other allies should focus on increasing pressure on Russia to shorten the war "and to secure Ukraine's freedom".

Trump's diesel deal is aimed at lowering fuel prices in America, which have risen following the US and Israel's conflict with Iran.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the agreement would allow Moscow to raise funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.

In response, Trump suggested Ukraine should "get a new leader" who could reach a deal with Russia to end the long-running conflict between the two countries.

Streeting said it was a matter for Ukrainians to choose their leader but added that the country was "fortunate to have someone of his calibre, his courage and his integrity leading their war effort".

He added that responsibility for the war "lies squarely and solely with President Putin and his imperialist ambitions".

The defence secretary said it was not the first time there had been public disagreements between Washington and Kyiv, adding: "In these situations we see it as our role and our responsibility to try and bring our friends back together again."

He also sought to emphasise the US's support for Ukraine, saying there was "often an understatement" of how much help they had provided.

"We're seeing US support for Ukraine in a number of ways from the provision of weapons - and we do a lot of procurement through the Americans - through to intelligence support and through the diplomatic initiative that Washington is leading."

Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says Trump

Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said Trump was "wrong" to call for Zelensky to go, adding: "The US is our closest ally but even close allies can disagree."

Speaking on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he also criticised the diesel deal saying it "sends out all the wrong messages".

"If you want a peaceful world, you don't do that sort of deal - you properly fund defence and prepare for war."

Also appearing on the programme, Streeting said the UK had to plan its defence spending on the basis that there could be a Russian attack on Nato - the military alliance made up of 32 countries - by 2030.

He said the UK didn't "seek conflict with Russia" but added: "Strength is the best form of deterrence."

Earlier this year, John Healey - now the chancellor - resigned as defence secretary accusing Sir Keir Starmer's government of not providing enough money for defence and said the UK had to be spending 3% of national income on defence by 2030, up from an estimated 2.6% this year.

Streeting said Healey would use the coming Budget to "plug" a £4.7bn funding gap to pay for the Defence Investment Plan.

He also said the government would set out a path to increase spending to 3.5% of national income by 2035 at next year's Spending Review.

Pressed on whether the government could commit to spending 3% of GDP by 2030, Streeting said he would "always push for more defence spending" but added: "We're not going to set out a spending commitment without showing how we will pay for it."

"If I were the chancellor to sit on your programme now and say '3% in 2030' without saying how we would pay for it, the markets would price in that risk and the cost of borrowing would go up."

stories.title: It's within DUP's gift to remove O'Neill as first minister, says Lockhart
stories.summary: Carla Lockhart says unionist voters are angry at Michelle O'Neill over her role in the Garvaghy Road protests.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
O'Neill previously dismissed a call from the DUP to resign over her role in protests against the Drumcree parade

Published 11 October 2026, 07:20 BST

A DUP MP says unionist voters are angry at Michelle O'Neill over her role in the Garvaghy Road protests and says it "cannot be business as usual" at Stormont.

Carla Lockhart said the DUP has it "within its gift to remove" O'Neill as Northern Ireland's first minister.

On Friday, the secretary of state banned the Portadown District Lodge from marching down the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road . His decision was welcomed by nationalist politicians but unionists have criticised the move.

O'Neill is one of a number of Sinn Féin politicians who have confirmed they received letters from the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) investigating protests over the Drumcree parading dispute.

What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? Published 29 September

Four key takeaways from the Drumcree dispute so far Published 21 hours ago

Speaking outside Drumcree Church on Saturday, Lockhart said her constituents are angry.

"They're angry at the chief constable for allowing lawlessness to win, for allowing the mob to dictate," she said.

"They're angry at the secretary of state for his intervention, but the most palpable anger is at Michelle O'Neill, this self-proclaimed 'first minister for all' for breaking the law flagrantly on the Garvaghy Road, and thumbing her nose at unionism and at the Orange Order and at this community."

Police had repeatedly warned those taking part in the unnotified protest that they could be liable for arrest.

O'Neill has defended her involvement, saying she was standing with the local community in opposition to an Orange Order parade through the area.

She previously dismissed a call from the DUP to resign over her role in protests telling the assembly she was "proud" to stand with the residents and "will continue to stand with them".

'It cannot be business as usual at Stormont'

Lockhart says her party must take action against O'Neill

The DUP (Democratic Unionist Party) share power with Sinn Féin in the Northern Ireland Executive, but Lockhart says it can no longer be business as usual.

"You can not continue to engage with someone who is so blatant in her disregard and disdain for a large section of this community," she said.

"Very clearly it cannot be business as usual at Stormont."

Lockhart says her party must take action against O'Neill.

"People want to see consequences, and we have said very clearly, profound consequence, and therefore we should use whatever is in our armoury to ensure that Michelle O'Neill, the person who really is supposed to be that first minister for all, as she claims, is dealt with in the appropriate way," she added.

The DUP could remove O'Neill from the first minister's position if the deputy first minister quits.

That role is held by Emma Little-Pengelly, but that seems unlikely.

DUP leader Gavin Robinson called on the chief constable to "be very open" in telling the public "what was the threat that he perceived"

DUP leader Gavin Robinson said that Lockhart "is right that the options are there", but stopped short of suggesting his party may collapse the executive.

Speaking on BBC News NI's Sunday Politics programme , he echoed Lockhart's words that "it will not be business as usual", but added: "does collapsing Stormont bring the Orangemen home"?

Robinson also called on the chief constable to "be very open" in telling the public "what was the threat that he perceived" when he asked the secretary of state to review the Parades Commission's determination.

He said he "certainly wouldn't" want Sir Chris to govern Northern Ireland if the executive did collapse.

TUV leader Jim Allister said he was "disappointed" by the DUP's "limp response".

He said Robinson promised "profound consequences, and then when he's asked what they are, it emerges that the Emperor of the DUP has no clothes".

Allister accused the DUP of "doing nothing", which he said showed "there are no political consequences" for Sinn Féin.

John O'Dowd was one of a number of Sinn Féin politicians who joined a protest with residents on the Garvaghy Road

Sinn Féin assembly member John O'Dowd rejected claims that the move to ban the parade went in favour of his party, saying "the decision went in the way of the residents" who he said have "faced an awful four weeks" since the application to walk was lodged.

O'Dowd, who is also finance minister in the executive, was one of a number of Sinn Féin politicians who joined a protest with residents on the Garvaghy Road.

On Thursday, the police said they had begun issuing letters inviting people "reasonably suspected" of committing offences linked to the protests to interview.

Speaking on BBC News NI's Sunday Politics programme , O'Dowd said: "I own my decision", adding that he thinks it was "the right thing to do".

"I got into politics to stand against the intimidation of communities such as the Garvaghy Road, who went through hell and high water over many, many years.

"I stood with the people of the Garvaghy Road. I will continue to stand with the people of Garvaghy Road because it was the right thing to do."

He added that he believes the community responded in "a peaceful, democratic way" to the decision to approve a march on 27 September.

"I would appeal, not only to Gavin, but maybe hopelessly to Carla and others, to calm their language and to show responsible leadership and calm leadership at this stage," he added.

"I don't think that continued demonisation or an attempt to criminalise the community of the Garvaghy Road is an appropriate way forward.

"What we need in Portadown is reconciliation."

Sir Chris Bryant said his decision to ban the Drumcree parade 'was in the best interests of peace'

The Parades Commission ruled that the march on Sunday 27 September could go ahead with restrictions in place.

That parade did not happen and, after a series of legal challenges and talks between residents and Orangemen, the secretary of state banned the procession on Friday.

Sir Chris Bryant said his decision to ban the Drumcree parade "was in the best interests of peace" .

The secretary of state said he received advice from the PSNI chief constable that allowing the procession to go ahead could lead to serious injury, disorder and wider unrest .

'It means something to me'

On Saturday, a High Court judge said a legal appeal by Orangemen following the secretary of state's decision was not an emergency case and adjourned the hearing until Monday.

Lockhart said the 35 Orangemen from Portadown District Lodge had "stood lawfully" for the last two weeks on Drumcree hill.

"I've been on this hill from I was 10 years of age, it means something to me. It means a lot to my constituents here in Upper Bann," she said.

So does the Upper Bann MP still have confidence in her own party?

"I have confidence that I will ensure that my constituents' voices are heard within the party, and I will ensure that I continue to represent the views here in Portadown," she said.

Published 11 October 2026, 01:44 BST

The government has launched a new taskforce to respond to extreme weather, including the risk of flooding this winter.

After a summer of record-breaking temperatures, the group will meet this week to assess how prepared the UK is for what the Met Office described as the "heightened potential" for wet, windy, stormy weather in the coming months.

"We're facing extreme weather, with flood and drought intertwined but the government is taking decisive action," Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) Minister Emma Hardy said in a statement ahead of the meeting.

The Environment Agency has warned approximately 6.3 million homes and businesses in England remain at risk of flooding.

Defra will host the first meeting on Wednesday, bringing together the Met Office, Environment Agency and mayoral authorities as well as the farming, water and insurance industries.

Hardy said: "This will put communities and businesses at the heart of our work and will make sure the UK is ready for whatever the weather brings next."

The government has committed at least £10.5bn until 2036 to protect homes, businesses and critical infrastructure from the growing threat of flooding.

The Met Office has said the current seasonal outlook suggests an increased likelihood of wetter than average conditions during autumn, in part due to the El Niño weather event.

It has warned that this year's iteration of the climate phenomenon is likely to be the strongest in living memory, with the peak not expected until the end of the year.

The Environment Agency has said that while flooding is not guaranteed, the odds of repeated storms, prolonged rain and saturated catchments are higher than average this winter.

It has urged households to check their flood risk, sign up to alerts and make a flood plan to prepare for any emergencies.

The warnings follow 12 months of extreme weather across the UK, with the summer of 2026 the country's hottest on record .

Last winter brought four named storms to the UK - Bram, Goretti, Ingrid and Chandra - and several significant flooding events, with the Met Office reporting that England received 42% more rainfall than its winter average.

As The Lucky Son picks up where Cunxin’s 2003 memoir left off, the renowned Chinese Australian ballet dancer reflects on sacrifices made by his wife, his years at a stockbroker, and his success leading the Queensland Ballet

Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email

S ome people live such extraordinary lives that a single autobiography simply won’t suffice. Li Cunxin has now written two. The renowned ballet dancer and former artistic director of Queensland Ballet had hoped he was finished writing his story after the phenomenal international success of his 2003 memoir, Mao’s Last Dancer. But life had other plans.

“Actually, I had signed a contract with Penguin Random House for a follow-up,” Cunxin says, from his home in Brisbane. “It was going to be about the lives of my brothers and friends in China, and the ways the country has changed over time. But then I was offered the job at Queensland Ballet and I had to dedicate all my time to that. I don’t think they were expecting [the sequel] to take 14 years!”

His second memoir, The Lucky Son, takes up precisely where Mao’s Last Dancer left off: as Cunxin and his ballet dancer wife Mary fly to their new lives at Houston Ballet under the directorship of Ben Stevenson. That outline of the proposed book on China can be glimpsed under the surface of this one, like a palimpsest; Cunxin’s six brothers’ lives are sketched, and a fascinating portrait of a country lifting itself from abject poverty to world superpower emerges.

“One of the things my mother taught me was to keep moving forward at all times,” Cunxin says. “Don’t think about the past, just concentrate on what is ahead.” That grit kept her children alive and was instrumental in shaping Cunxin’s dogged, highly ambitious personality.

Determination runs in the family. Mary was a deeply respected dancer herself, a career she sacrificed when she and Cunxin discovered their daughter Sophie was born profoundly deaf. “We were so fearful that Sophie would miss out on so much,” Cunxin says. “Music and dance and all the magical things.”

Mary immediately left the world of ballet (she would return years later as ballet mistress at Queensland Ballet) to teach Sophie to talk. “Mary was incredible,” Cunxin recalls. “She gave everything to the task.”

One one hand, it was a complete success. Sophie was fitted with a bionic ear (then known as a cochlear implant) and thrived; she embraced dance, had a successful education and excelled in the workplace. Cunxin and Mary assumed they’d done all that was needed.

But then in 2015, Sophie sent an email to her parents that shocked and devastated them. Sophie expressed frustration at her parents for wanting their daughter to hear; she felt she’d come halfway to meet their world, but they had not met hers. They had not even bothered to learn sign language. Her “deafness was her birthright”, Cunxin writes in the book. Now, he says, Sophie “is a kind of ambassador between the hearing and deaf communities”. And he and Mary have begun learning Auslan.

Cunxin’s dance career was so exemplary – moving from the Beijing Dance Academy to Houston Ballet, and then to principal artist at Australian Ballet – he could have been forgiven for hanging up his pointe shoes and walking into a lucrative position in a stockbroking firm. Indeed, that’s exactly what he did. An unsuccessful tilt at the artistic directorship of Australian Ballet (the role eventually went to David McAllister) utterly crushed him, and it seemed for a few years he would never return to the world of professional ballet.

Of course, that wasn’t how it panned out: despite being burned by that failure, Cunxin reluctantly put his name in the hat when Queensland Ballet were looking for their next artistic director. That tenacity and resolve was once more poured into the theatre.

“To be a leader of any kind takes vision,” Cunxin says. “I had a very strong vision for Queensland Ballet. But you also have to be a good communicator, because you need to inspire others to join in your vision.” And you need to apply yourself, which wasn’t such an issue for someone trained at Beijing Dance Academy, with its brutal rehearsal regime and exacting standards.

One of the delights of The Lucky Son is the way it tracks some of our favourite characters from Mao’s Last Dancer, including The Bandit, Cunxin’s bestie at the Beijing Dance Academy; his gorgeous instructor Teacher Xiao; and his astonishing mum and dad, Niang and Dia. There are echoes in the events too: Stevenson’s trip to Queensland to watch his protégé mount Cinderella recalls the unforgettable moment in Mao’s Last Dancer when his parents leave China for the first time to see their son dance and the audience gives them a standing ovation.

Central to Cunxin’s success at Queensland Ballet – where he oversaw a massive improvement in standards and built a stunning new home for the company, the Thomas Dixon Centre – were the lessons he learned from his time away from ballet, when he was a stockbroker: “I learned so much from the business world – when we had to approach donors for money, I could speak their language.” Relationships with Elisabeth Murdoch and the Ian Potter Foundation came in handy, and he and Mary also contributed some money of their own. It’s now a world-class organisation.

Looking back on his life now, Cunxin feels an overwhelming sense of “gratitude, for the opportunities I was given and the people and artists who shaped me”. The Lucky Son concludes on stage – hardly surprising, given so many of the key moments in Cunxin’s life have been there – but this time it is in Switzerland, where he was awarded ballet’s most prestigious award, the Prix de Lausanne, in 2025.

After a few years of serious health issues (Mary is a cancer survivor and Cunxin has a major heart condition), the couple are increasingly happy to chill. “Our health has forced us to slow down,” he says with the emphasis on forced, as if there were no way they would slow down on purpose. “I worked very hard for two years on this book – it’s been all-consuming. So yes, I am enjoying taking things a little slower.” Is he confident that ballet will survive the coming AI tsunami, given how hard the art form is to perfect and how much time and effort is required? “I am worried, but I do think ballet is special,” he says. “When people come to see ballet, they are blown away by the artistry, the physicality and the music. I think it’s more important than ever to connect people.”

The Lucky Son by Li Cunxin is out now (Penguin, $36.99)

Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs

The EU said it has reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.

Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations with China since June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers.

The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday.

“It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place.

China has been flooding Europe with cars , including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers. Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery. They are sold by carmakers as a transitional step towards BEVs.

Šefčovič said the Chinese had recognised the political pressure building in every member state in Europe with “literally thousands of job losses” at risk because of the flood of cheap imports from China across many sectors including chemicals and textiles.

He said EU leaders were “clearly expecting very fast action” from the European Commission and the Chinese recognised that.

“I am glad to say that the Chinese partners appreciated this very strong political argument, and therefore, we can proceed through the negotiated solution,” he said.

“This ‌is far from the end. It’s a crucial first step, but only a first step,” Šefčovič told ‌reporters in Beijing where he had travelled to hold ​talks with his Chinese counterpart.

Earlier this week senior EU officials said they were heading to Beijing to seek what they called a “proof of concept” or pilot scheme with one sector which they hoped could then be expanded to other areas under pressure from Chinese competition.

Šefčovič said he put “so much emphasis” on the negotiations because it was “very difficult to stop” a trade war once it was declared.

As part of a 16-point agreement, Beijing and Brussels will continue negotiating on cars, export restrictions on rare earths and access to China for more food and drink from the EU.

China said both sides would adhere to “procedures concerning company price undertakings” for hybrid cars suggesting one method of curbing sales would be to set higher minimum price tags for Chinese cars sold in Europe.

The EU commissioner will brief EU diplomats in Brussels on Sunday ahead of a leaders’ summit on Thursday.

A statement from the Chinese ministry of commerce said China is “willing … to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU”.

It added that both sides had “reaffirmed their commitment … to properly handle differences within the framework of WTO rules, and to continuing to stabilise and balance bilateral trade and economic relations”.

While China and the EU acknowledged “differences” between them it appears that China has accepted the EU’s request to create a new model for trade balances starting with a pilot on hybrid cars.

Trump continued: "Both parties have agreed," before urging restraint from both Kyiv and Moscow: "Do not break it!"

There was ‌no immediate ​confirmation ⁠from from the warring parties.

Russia has repeatedly struck Ukraine's power plants and transmission lines around Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa and elsewhere, to lower civilian morale, especially during the winter months.

Recently, Ukraine has stepped up long-range strikes deep inside Russian territory, targeting major oil refineries and other facilities to curb Moscow's refining capacity and fuel supplies.

stories.title: Germany sticks to Russia sanctions after Trump diesel deal
stories.summary: After Washington announced a sanctions pause on Russian diesel, Germany has said it remains committed to pressuring Moscow and supporting Ukraine. More on DW.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
After Washington announced a sanctions pause on Russian diesel, Germany has said it remains committed to pressuring Moscow and supporting Ukraine. More on DW.

What you need to know

Merz's CDU gathers for leadership meeting addressing electoral free fall

The German government has said it will continue working with EU partners on Russia sanctions

Ex-Chancellor Schröder faces criticism for attending Putin's birthday

'Ragebait' voted Germany's youth word of the year

Read below for a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Saturday, October 10, and Sunday, October 11.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Deutsche Bank CEO: Political extremism putting off foreign investors

Christian Sewing, CEO of Deutsche Bank , Germany's biggest, warned that the growing strength of both the far right and the far left is spooking foreign investors.

Sewing told the tabloid Bild that recent election victories for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and post-communist Left Party "pose a significant risk for Germany and should not be downplayed."

The Deutsche Bank boss said it mattered little that the elections were on the state and local level. "You can't expect a foreign investor to immediately draw a distinction ‌between a state government and Germany as a whole," he ‌said.

"It's ​seen as Germany as a whole and I think that from an investor's point of view, that's understandable."

Some economists say the AfD is creating an atmosphere that will drive away much needed skilled labor as well as foreign investors.

The Left Party, meanwhile, won victory in Berlin promising to expropriate residential property companies' holdings to lower housing costs in the German capital.

"Whether ​it's Saxony-Anhalt with ⁠the AfD or what's happening here in Berlin," said Sewing, "it's anything but conducive to economic growth. ⁠And it's anything ​but investment-friendly."

Sewing said Chancellor Friedrich Merz must get on with carrying out reforms and reviving the economy, saying, "That is the only response we have to the far-right and far-left extremists in this country."

Foreign Minister Wadephul: 'Germany fully supports' Zelenskyy

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Sunday made clear that Berlin stands with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, rejecting US President Donald Trump's calls for his replacement.

Germany will "fully support the president as he carries out his difficult ​duties," said Wadephul at his party's two-day CDU leadership conference.

On Friday, after a long phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump announced a deal that would see sanctions on Russia eased dramatically and allow Moscow to export millions of barrels of diesel , thus pumping much needed cash into Russia's economy.

On Saturday, Trump called for Zelenskyy's removal and again sought to pin blame on the Ukrainian president — not his own Iran war — for high global oil prices.

Germany is the biggest EU donor to Ukraine, and an advocate for tighter sanctions and increased pressure on Russia to end its war against Ukraine.

Berlin responded to Trump's oil scheme by stating that it would not be lifting any Russian sanctions .

On Sunday, Wadephul responded to the second point, making the case for "consistency and clarity" in terms of support for Ukraine.

"We ‌don't need less pressure on Putin to force him ​to negotiate," ⁠said the German diplomat. "We need more," he added. "That is what this moment requires and that's what this government stands for."

Merz's CDU huddles to find way out of electoral free fall

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz 's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) will kick off a two-day leadership meeting on Sunday to plot a path out of the electoral crisis the party finds itself in after three dismal state elections.

The 25-member leadership meeting was called after the CDU — until now one of Germany's two largest popular parties — failed to even clear the 5% hurdle to enter Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's state legislature . The stinging loss, which Merz himself described as "a disaster," represented the first time in the party's history that it was booted from a statehouse.

The CDU has been struggling to hold off the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party and has been thrust into an identity crisis due to the rate at which it is losing voters to the party.

In one of the summer's other elections — in Saxony-Anhalt — the CDU dropped nearly 20 percentage points, getting clobbered by the AfD, which racked up over 40% of the vote.

Merz under pressure: CDU lawmaker on election setbacks

This weekend's meeting is designed to address voter dissatisfaction with the CDU-led governing coalition with the Social Democrats (SPD), as well as looking at possible long-term solutions to the party's electoral death spiral.

Faced with this new electoral reality, leaders will reportedly look at the potential policy consequences of the party's losses, reconsidering whether to push on with much-needed reforms to the healthcare and retirement systems, for instance.

Party leaders will also grapple with the fundamental question of how to deal with the AfD in the long run, namely, whether to maintain the party's "firewall" policy rejecting any cooperation or to work with the anti-immigrant rightwing populists in hopes of remaining relevant.

Speaking with Germany's Welt am Sonntag newspaper ahead of the pow-wow, Hesse State Premier Boris Rhein said leadership, "has to deal with all of the issues that are important to everyday citizens: Cost of living, security, immigration and jobs."

This blog is on pause

We are pausing our coverage for now. Join us again on Sunday morning for more coverage of the German news and analysis.

Germany rejects proposed EU budget, calls for greater cuts

Germany swiftly rejected a proposed new budget for the European Union that was put forward on Saturday.

Ireland, which holds the rotating EU presidency, put forward a budget of €1.826 trillion ($2.046 trillion) for the next seven years — a reduction of around €159 billion compared to the European Commission's original proposal of nearly €1.985 trillion.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the budget cuts should go further .

"The size of the new proposal is no basis for an agreement," Merz said.

"The EU ​budget must be affordable for ⁠those who bear the main burden of financing," he added.

Germany is the largest net contributor to the EU budget. It and other net contributors including the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, Austria and Finland all want the next budget to be slashed by hundreds of billions of euros.

But the second-largest net contributor to the EU budget, France, has instead argued that the 27-member bloc needs a more generous budget in order to overcome new challenges.

'Ragebait' named Germany's 2026 Youth Word of the Year

The Langenscheidt publishing house on Saturday named "ragebait" as Germany's 2026 Youth Word of the Year during the Frankfurt Book Fair.

Ragebait is social media content designed to draw people in by making them angry with provocative claims, lies, or outrageous opinions, thereby driving up clicks and interactions.

Langenscheidt, Germany's best-selling dictionary publisher, organized an online poll with 1 million young people taking part in this year's competition.

Ragebait took 36.5% of the vote, with runners-up including the terms "peak," meaning the best of the best, and "crashout," meaning when someone loses their cool.

Germany 'committed' to further Russia sanctions

Germany on Saturday said it would continue pursuing sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine, coming a day after US President Donald Trump announced a temporary US sanctions reprieve on Russian diesel.

"The federal ⁠government ⁠has taken note of the US decision relating to Russian diesel deliveries," government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said in a statement.

"The federal government ​remains committed to the decisions on ​sanctions against ‌Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions," the statement added.

Germany's "support for Ukraine in its struggle to defend itself remains unfailing ... Diplomatic efforts for a peaceful solution continue," he added.

After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow has been subject to round after round of sanctions packages led by the US and EU.

Russian crude and other oil products have been subject to EU sanctions since 2023, and Germany has not imported any oil or oil products from Russia since then.

A spokesperson for Economic Affairs Minister Katherina Reiche said Saturday that "Germany stands fully behind the sanctions packages."

" Our supply is diversified in this area; we are independent of Russian oil," the spokesperson said.

Germany remains Ukraine's largest financial backer in Europe. During a visit to Kyiv last weekend, Chancellor Friedrich Merz reiterated Germany's unwavering support for Ukraine.

In what amounts to a major reversal in US policy, Trump on Friday said he would temporarily lift US sanctions to allow Russia to "immediately" supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to US and global markets.

The move comes as diesel prices reach record levels after the war in Iran launched by the US and Israel sent diesel prices skyrocketing around the world. In the US, the high prices are putting political pressure on Trump's Republicans ahead of the midterm elections in November.

However, despite Trump's claims on social media, it remains unclear how much Russian fuel will reach global markets amid domestic fuel shortages as Ukraine continues to target refineries.

Ex-Chancellor Schröder criticized for Putin birthday visit

The appearance of Germany's Russia-friendly former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder at President Vladimir Putin's birthday party earlier this week has drawn criticism in Germany.

Franziska Brantner, the co-leader of Germany's Green party, called on Schröder's Social Democrats (SPD) to revisit revoking Schröder's party membership.

"Russia is now even attacking us in Germany with hybrid attacks. Schröder hasn't learned anything from this. A new approach needs to be put on the table," she told the Tagesspiegel newspaper.

"Schröder is celebrating Putin's birthday with him, while civilians in Ukraine are once again dying as a result of Russian attacks. This is politically unacceptable," said Brantner.

Anything less than expulsion from the party would be "a disastrous signal, not only to Ukraine but also to the people and their safety in our country," Brantner added.

The SPD's Hubertus Heil, who served as Germany's labor minister from 2018 to 2025, also criticized Schröder.

"The warm embrace between Schröder and Putin in Moscow deeply outrages and disturbs me," Heil told the Tagesspiegel .

Celebrating with a "dictator" whose "murderous imperialism causes horrific suffering every day" is "unjustifiable under any circumstances," he said.

Putin celebrated his 74th birthday in Moscow on Wednesday. The Kremlin said Putin learned that Schröder was on a business trip in the Russian capital via Russian media reports.

"The president invited his old friend to his home," the Kremlin said, with the Russian government releasing pictures of Schröder and Putin smiling and clasping hands,

Schröder's business and personal ties to Russia have drawn controversy since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Schröder's tax-payer financed Berlin office was closed in 2022 over his involvement in the Russian energy sector, but he fended off calls at the time by fellow party members to be expelled from the SPD.

stories.title: Resisting the Menace of Federal Data Consolidation
stories.summary: In the past two years, the federal government has unlawfully consolidated data exposing our private information. This consolidation has been chaotic but generally came in three rolling waves: It started with DOGE, moved to agency-to-agency data sharing with ICE, and then attempted data-driven purges of state voter rolls. We all deserve to live in a world where the data we use to pay our taxes, receive benefits, and vote is not combined and weaponized against us. The amalgamation of data leads to mistakes, abuses, and a lack of trust in institutions meant to protect us. Overall, it can chill our participation in society. This is particularly true for groups disfavored by this administration—especially immigrants and protesters. Congress highlighted similar abuses—including the creation of enemies lists and snooping on activists and federal employees—following the McCarthy and Watergate eras. And the increasing use of computers to magnify those harms led Congress to pass a slate of protections like the federal Privacy Act of 1974. The good news is that many people have stepped forward to resist the federal government’s unprecedented and unlawful data consolidations. Many groups, including EFF, have filed lawsuits to enforce our data privacy laws, and many states have, too. Legislators at the federal and state levels have worked to expose and oppose these surveillance programs. And many people have protested for their right to data privacy. Existing data privacy protections have been essential in the past two years, but they can be improved . This should include: narrowing loopholes and increasing enforcement in existing laws, limiting the government’s purchase of data on the commercial market, and passing a comprehensive consumer privacy law. Data Consolidation by DOGE Starting on January 20, 2025, President Trump created DOGE —essentially renaming an existing agency originally meant to modernize government technology. Rather than engage in modernization, DOGE quickly obtained high-level access to sensitive databases across the government that store millions of people’s personal records—including at the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), the Social Security Administration , and the Treasury Department . stories.title: Organizing in the Town at Oakland Tech Week
stories.summary: EFF was thrilled to join organizers, advocates, and activists in the East Bay for the second annual Oakland Tech Week last week. We are grateful to our friends at MediaJustice and Upturn for inviting us co-present this all-day event, “Building Beyond Big Tech: Organizing Oakland’s Future” , on Sept. 30. The event, hosted by the Kapor Center in downtown Oakland, offered a unique chance to spend time with people across The Town and the Bay Area working to create a better future for everyone. “We’re at this truly consequential moment,” said EFF executive director Nicole Ozer, in her speech kicking off the day’s events. “We know that in this community’s work—and communities across the country—our ability to ensure that technology empowers rather than oppresses is fundamental to the future of countries, our livelihoods, and, literally, our lives.” We also participated in a panel on the state of play in California, moderated by MediaJustice executive director Steven Renderos. Director of State Affairs Hayley Tsukayama joined reporter Khari Johnson of CalMatters and Crystal Zemero of People Over Billionaires to talk about the landscape at the state level. stories.title: Fixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilation | Simon Tisdall
stories.summary: This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing ‘end times’ closer by the day Humankind has fearfully and sometimes joyfully anticipated the end of the world ever since it began. The Bible’s Book of Revelation speaks of “end times”, a period of tribulation, war, famine, plague, floods and environmental catastrophe that may seem a less absurd prospect today than perhaps it once did. Islam, too, posits a fateful day of judgment or day of reckoning. Christian evangelicals believe that, in the final rapture, a chosen few – the righteous or the “elect” – will be saved while sinners burn. It’s a minority view. Matthew’s gospel predicts most people will defy, ignore or ridicule warnings of imminent Armageddon. Peter, another of Jesus’s disciples, agreed: “In the last days, scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires.” Yet such worldly scepticism does not mean a universal cataclysm is less likely. It may make it more probable. Donald Trump’s blanket denials of the dangers ostensibly posed by artificial intelligence, whose uncontrolled development is seen by some as the latest harbinger of apocalypse , could be interpreted as fulfilling Peter’s prophecy. This US president, the nearest thing the world has to a one-man doomsday machine, is a great one for scoffing and evil desires. In Robert Harris’s 2019 novel, The Second Sleep, a worried scientist lists half a dozen ways the world might end. They include devastating climate change, pandemic disease, a giant asteroid collision with Earth, or some other overwhelming calamity. Few heed the fictional scientist’s fears. In the event, what destroys him and almost everybody else is a disturbingly plausible cyber crash – a global digital and internet meltdown. stories.summary: Jeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions Trump Here is a film for all those people who solemnly deplore social media in conversation but haven’t quite got round to deleting their accounts. Sixteen years have gone by since The Social Network , written by Aaron Sorkin and directed by David Fincher; this was the addictive, obsessive-compulsive movie about the birth of Facebook in Harvard’s macho-competitive cauldron of student sexism and nerdy self-pity, starring Jesse Eisenberg as the fast-talking, arrogant, not-necessarily-evil genius Mark Zuckerberg. Now Sorkin is back with a sequel of sorts, directing his own script – and now Zuckerberg is basically evil, but also weirdly slow talking, as if all the zinging, smart-alecky Sorkinesque dialogue energy of the first film has been siphoned away in early middle age and dispersed among the insurgents in the new cast. Sorkin’s jittery, funny, syncopated style is unmistakable, as distinctive in its way as David Mamet, although he has one joke about “spatula” being a Yiddish word that he has borrowed from Philip Roth’s Portnoy’s Complaint . It is the story of how in 2021, Zuckerberg’s Facebook empire was challenged by courageous whistleblower-employee Frances Haugen and Wall Street Journal investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz, who were on a mission to tell the world how Zuckerberg, scared by falling revenue, changed the algorithm so that engagement was supercharged by rage bait and hate speech, malice and envy. Facebook, moreover, didn’t factcheck political ads, thus driving a huge, nationwide surge in extremist groups and teen bullying and becoming a major player in the Capitol riots. stories.summary: Ukraine's president sharply criticised the move, calling it an "investment in war that must be ended, not prolonged".

stories.body:
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met in Alaska last year

Published 9 October 2026

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has condemned Donald Trump's announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel into the US.

Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged", a position quickly backed by Ukraine's European allies.

Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and a further one million after that.

It is understood that the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.

Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period", dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine.

Putin later said that Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts.

Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror".

"We count on America's fair support for our defence of life, for our defence of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one," he wrote.

He later pointed to deadly overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv as Russia expressing "its thanks" for the agreement.

Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.

Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Published 1 day ago

Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15 people Published 18 hours ago

Tim Armitage, an investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot, said the numbers mentioned by Trump were "relatively small".

He said the first tranche equated to approximately 2.25 million barrels, and daily US consumption was around 3.8 million barrels, "so it won't make a material difference to pump prices in the US".

"Granted, there are then two more releases to come, but it does appear to be a slightly desperate move by President Trump to try to lower inflation ahead of the midterms," he said.

Paul Johnson, former director of the Institute of Fiscal Studies think tank and provost of The Queen's College, Oxford, said: "What would make a difference, of course, is sorting out what's happening with Iran.

"Let's be clear, President Trump has created this problem himself," he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

"This is a problem not created because of Ukraine and Russia in terms of diesel prices at the moment, this is created by the war in the Middle East."

The BBC has asked the White House what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment.

The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine.

The EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't."

She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday.

Meanwhile, a UK government spokesperson said its position "could not be clearer" and that it would continue working with international partners to support Ukraine and bring about sustained peace.

"We will also maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK, increasing the cost of Putin's aggression and supporting efforts to secure a just and lasting peace."

Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.

That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.

Ukraine's President Volodymr Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror"

The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.

Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market.

Putin said he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large."

An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."

Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. Its diesel production has fallen by nearly 30%, according to International Energy Agency estimates.

Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices.

But Zelensky defended the strikes on Friday, saying they were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector".

"Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said.

Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? Published 1 day ago

Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, and the details of exactly how Russia will supply this fuel to the global market is unclear.

But the announced deal represents a remarkable about-face, as the US Congress recently enacted legislation - signed by the president - to authorise new American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.

What impact the deal with Russia will have on fuel prices also remains unclear. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, remains above $103 a barrel. Before the war with Iran, Brent crude was trading at about $73 a barrel.

With the looming US elections - which will determine whether Republicans maintain control of Congress - Trump has been searching for ways to ease his Republican party's political pain.

Earlier this week, he said he was "thinking about" suspending the federal tax on gasoline and also announced that he would allow so-called red dye diesel to be used on US highways without facing federal tax.

Trump has also successfully pressured G7 nations into releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to help ease supply concerns and previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.

Published 9 October 2026

Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.

Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.

Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.

The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.

As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured.

The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.

It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.

Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky criticises 'gift to Putin' Published 1 day ago

What are the US midterms? A simple guide Published 5 days ago

For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.

He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves . He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.

He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.

His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.

Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear.

It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy".

"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.

It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.

The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.

Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.

The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.

Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.

With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked.

"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.

But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.

Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.
